pages.x: The Soviet Union was made up of fifteen republics, from Estonia on the Baltic to Kazakhstan in Central Asia, home to over a hundred peoples, all ruled from Moscow. When Gorbachev's openness let people speak freely, old wounds came out: the famine in Ukraine, Stalin's deportations, the seizure of the Baltic states in 1940. And the shops were empty.

On 23 August 1989, fifty years after Hitler and Stalin secretly agreed to divide Eastern Europe between them, about two million Estonians, Latvians and Lithuanians joined hands in a human chain 675 kilometres long, from Tallinn through Riga to Vilnius, to demand their freedom.

In March 1990 Lithuania declared itself independent, the first republic to break away. In January 1991 Soviet troops stormed the television tower in Vilnius, and 14 people were killed as unarmed crowds tried to block the tanks. Instead of crushing the Baltic peoples, the attack hardened them, and Moscow drew back.

In August 1991 hardliners in Moscow, afraid the union was about to break up, held Gorbachev prisoner at his holiday home in Crimea and sent tanks into the capital. Boris Yeltsin, the elected president of Russia, climbed onto a tank outside the parliament and called on the people to resist. Crowds built barricades, soldiers would not shoot, and in three days the coup collapsed.

After the coup the republics declared independence one after another. The decisive vote came on 1 December 1991, when more than 90 per cent of Ukrainians chose independence. A week later the leaders of Russia, Ukraine and Belarus met at a hunting lodge in a Belarusian forest and signed a paper saying that the Soviet Union had ceased to exist.

On 25 December 1991 Gorbachev resigned in a short speech on television. That evening the red Soviet flag over the Kremlin was lowered for the last time, and the white, blue and red flag of Russia raised in its place. The next day the Soviet parliament voted the union out of existence.

In Russia prices soared as the old system was scrapped, and people's savings vanished. Pensioners sold their belongings in the street, and life expectancy for Russian men fell below 58. A few well-connected men, the oligarchs, bought up the country's oil and metals for a fraction of their worth. Wars broke out in Chechnya, Georgia, Moldova and Tajikistan, and between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

The end of the Soviet Union finished the Cold War and left hundreds of millions of people free to choose their own way, with less bloodshed than anyone had feared. Vladimir Putin later called it the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the century. Many of its quarrels, above all between Russia and Ukraine, were never settled.
pts: Fifteen countries were born from one
The August coup collapsed in three days
The red flag came down on 25 December 1991
